impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement possessed an exclusionary right sufficient to satisfy Article III's irreducible constitutional minimum of standing. The court found the retained litigation right was not rendered illusory by the rights granted to the licensee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners can structure exclusive licenses that retain meaningful enforcement rights, providing flexibility to license commercialization while preserving the ability to independently police infringement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face broader exposure to patent suits from licensors who have transferred most commercial rights but retained litigation authority under carefully drafted agreements.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache treatment patents covering anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, which are the basis for Teva's Ajovy product and compete with Lilly's migraine treatments. The court found the district court erred in its written-description and enablement analysis, reinstating a jury verdict of willful infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders benefit from a more favorable standard for written description and enablement of antibody claims, strengthening protection for biologics where the specification discloses methods known in the art for making claimed antibodies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar drug manufacturers face stronger patent barriers in the anti-CGRP antibody space and potentially broader genus claims in biologics patents.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by emulating a program and comparing function calls to a model are directed to abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and the Alice framework, and whether damages can be based on foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million judgment, holding that Columbia's cybersecurity patents claiming methods for detecting anomalous program executions were abstract at Alice step one and required further proceedings on step two. The court also held the district court erred in allowing damages based on Norton's foreign sales and reversed a contempt order against Norton's counsel Quinn Emanuel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against cybersecurity patent assertions gain stronger § 101 eligibility defenses, and the foreign sales ruling limits damages exposure for globally sold software products.
impacts.negativeImplications: University and research institution patent holders face heightened eligibility challenges for software-related security patents, and patent plaintiffs may not recover damages based on foreign sales of accused products.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's finding that asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law was supported by legally sufficient evidence, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed trade secret misappropriation findings, holding there was insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets related to cosmetic penile implants were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed patent inventorship findings, holding that generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from rigorous evidentiary requirements showing claimed secrets actually derive independent economic value from not being generally known, providing stronger defenses against overbroad trade secret claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face higher burdens in establishing protectability, particularly where the claimed secrets relate to concepts available in the public domain, even if combined in novel ways.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether summary judgment was proper on inequitable conduct in patent prosecution and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim based on the same alleged misconduct before the PTO.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct (which had been granted against Tenaris) and a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim (which had been granted against Global Tubing), finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether Tenaris engaged in inequitable conduct in obtaining coiled tubing patents and whether such conduct rose to the level of antitrust fraud supporting attempted monopolization claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of inequitable conduct benefit from the court's recognition that material factual disputes preclude summary resolution, and patent challengers retain viable Walker Process antitrust claims where evidence of intent to deceive the PTO exists.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face continued risk that allegations of undisclosed prior art during prosecution could support both unenforceability and antitrust liability, creating dual exposure in competitive industries.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to selecting a processor core with the fastest measured processing speed to run a task that cannot be run across multiple cores are limited to domestic conduct, and whether doctrine of equivalents infringement was properly rejected.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent, holding that the district court erred in its extraterritoriality analysis and in rejecting VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory. The court affirmed the striking of certain damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against semiconductor and processor technologies benefit from a broader view of domestic infringement for products designed and partially tested in the U.S., even when final testing or manufacture occurs abroad.
impacts.negativeImplications: Chip manufacturers face expanded infringement exposure for multicore processor technologies and must carefully evaluate domestic conduct in their design and testing processes.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility rulings for certain constellation design patents while affirming others, creating a split outcome on § 101 eligibility for communication system patents. The court affirmed infringement and damages findings, including the denial of JMOL challenging Constellation's damages expert testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in digital communications may rely on claims tied to specific hardware implementations (transmitters/receivers) as more likely to survive § 101 challenges, and damages methodologies tied to standards-essential technologies were upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers like LG face continued infringement exposure on communication standard patents, and the split eligibility ruling creates uncertainty for patents claiming constellation designs at varying levels of abstraction.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify to facts outside personal knowledge for purposes of establishing the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representatives may testify beyond their personal knowledge and that computer source code describing commands is not hearsay. The court rejected arguments that the on-sale bar requires express disclosure of a device's functionality at the time of sale.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers benefit from broader admissibility of corporate deposition testimony and source code evidence when proving prior art sales, even when the corporate witness joined the company after the relevant events.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face expanded on-sale bar risks, as prior commercial sales of products can invalidate later patents even without contemporaneous disclosure of the product's specific functionality to the public.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on the absence of a quantified remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of a patent plaintiff's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment for Microsoft on absence-of-remedy grounds. The court held that the district court applied an overly rigid standard in excluding the damages opinion and erred in denying the motion to reopen discovery, effectively denying the patentee any opportunity to present its case.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more forgiving standard for damages expert reports, and courts must provide reasonable opportunities for patentees to cure deficiencies rather than summarily disposing of cases on remedy grounds.
impacts.negativeImplications: Large technology companies like Microsoft may face prolonged patent litigation where damages theories that might otherwise be excluded are given additional opportunities for refinement.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features infringed Masimo's patents for user-worn noninvasive physiological measurement devices, and whether Masimo established a domestic industry.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watch models infringing Masimo's blood oximetry patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing devices. The court found no error in the Commission's validity, infringement, or domestic industry determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in wearable health technology can effectively use ITC proceedings to obtain import exclusion orders against major competitors, providing powerful enforcement beyond district court remedies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics companies incorporating health-monitoring features face significant import ban risks from ITC proceedings, potentially requiring product redesigns or licensing agreements to maintain market access.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after missing the deadline for seeking a stay of an earlier-filed action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that a party cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for mandatory stays under § 1659(a)(2) by voluntarily dismissing an original declaratory judgment action and refiling a new one. The court ruled that BioMarin could not obtain a mandatory stay of Ascendis's refiled DJ action after having missed the 30-day deadline in the original action.
impacts.positiveImplications: Declaratory judgment plaintiffs are protected from gamesmanship by ITC respondents seeking to delay parallel district court proceedings through tactical dismissal and refiling of actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day window for seeking a mandatory stay of parallel district court proceedings cannot cure the deficiency by refiling, requiring more careful monitoring of statutory deadlines.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination where it failed to adequately address claim limitations requiring reporting sensor information after a predetermined time delay, and whether a non-party to underlying litigation can file IPR petitions on behalf of a time-barred party.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness finding regarding FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent, holding the Board failed to adequately address specific claim limitations related to delayed reporting of sensor information. The court also addressed concerns about potential abuse of the IPR system where Qualcomm filed petitions challenging patents asserted against Roambee on the last day of Roambee's filing deadline.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from requirements that the PTAB must thoroughly address each claim limitation in obviousness determinations, providing stronger protection against conclusory invalidity findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies using third parties to file IPR petitions face increased scrutiny and potential procedural barriers when the timing suggests coordination with a time-barred litigant.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary exceeded statutory authority by using PACER fees to fund unrelated court technology programs. The court upheld attorneys' fees, costs, and incentive awards to three nonprofit class representatives, finding the settlement provided full or substantial reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement establishes that government fee programs must stay within statutory bounds, and class action settlements providing near-full reimbursement to class members will be upheld even over objections regarding fee awards and incentive payments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Government agencies and the federal judiciary face liability exposure when fee programs are used to cross-subsidize unrelated operations, and the precedent may encourage similar challenges to other government fee structures.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patentee was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed noninfringement of Actelion's epoprostenol (Veletri) formulation patents, holding that the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at the standard ambient temperature of 25°C recognized in the field. The court also upheld the bar on Actelion's doctrine of equivalents theory.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from precise claim construction tied to industry-standard measurement conditions, providing clearer design-around guidance for ANDA filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent scope when claims use scientific measurements without specifying conditions, as courts will apply field-standard measurement parameters.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly determined that a competitor's redesigned products did not infringe asserted patents for wet dry surface cleaning devices, and whether the complainant established a technical domestic industry.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's determination in full, upholding both the exclusion order against Tineco's original infringing wet-dry cleaning products and the finding that Tineco's redesigned products did not infringe. The court also affirmed Bissell's technical domestic industry and rejected Tineco's cross-appeal challenges to infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies subject to ITC exclusion orders can successfully design around patented technology, and the decision validates the ITC's approach to evaluating redesigned products in Section 337 investigations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders may find that ITC exclusion orders have limited long-term effectiveness when competitors can redesign products to avoid infringement while maintaining market presence.
